To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) search engines' optimal strategies are to rank ads according to their revenue potential, (ii) advertisers are willing to pay a premium for a higher rank, but only if this will increase the number of clicks, (iii) search engines' revenue is not a good proxy for the value of an ad rank, and (iv) search engines should rank ads according to the revenue they generate, but should not use this ranking as the only criterion, and should consider the number of clicks as

the ranking strategy of search engines is a function of their relative size, the price elasticity of the demand of advertisers for their advertising services, the relative cost of advertising on the two search engines and their relative size.

search engines' ranking rules are determined by the advertisers' behavior and that Yahoo! has been right to switch from a bid-based ranking strategy to a revenue-based ranking strategy, as this strategy is optimal when advertisers are not strategic.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the strategic interaction between advertisers and search engines.
the strategic interaction between two players: the search engine and the advertiser.
the strategic interaction between search engines and advertisers, in the context of sponsored search engines.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ranking strategy of a search engine is determined by the relative market share of the search engine.
Yahoo!'s move is a rational one.
the ranking rules are not only a matter of search engine's preferences, but are the outcome of the competition between search engines.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the search engine ranking strategy depends on the advertisers behavior and that this behavior in turn depends on the search engines strategy.

the search engine that has a larger market share will be able to implement a revenue-based ranking, and the other search engine will be able to do so when the difference of market shares becomes sufficiently large.
we show that the competition between search engines is more subtle than it may seem at first.
The main takeaway from our work is that
search engines should not only consider their revenue, but also how the advertisers are reacting to their strategies, in particular how their ranking rule affects the advertisers' behavior.
the search engine's ranking rule strategy has to be determined by the search engine's market share.
the search engine that implements a revenue-based ranking strategy can be more profitable than the search engine implementing the bid-based strategy.
